The evidence, however, indicated that the accused had assaulted the woman's daughter-in-law to outrage her modesty. The accused defended himself against the charge of assaulting the woman and focused his cross-examination on proving that he did not assault or outrage the modesty of the woman. The prosecution's case was that the accused had touched and caught the hand of the daughter-in-law and fled when she raised an alarm. The trial court convicted the accused under sections 452 and 354 of the IPC, but the High Court upheld the conviction. The Supreme Court, however, held that the charge was incorrect as it did not mention the daughter-in-law, and the accused was not aware of the charge against her. The Court concluded that the accused was prejudiced by the error in the charge and directed a new trial after framing a charge against the daughter-in-law.

On the way, he was restrained by the accused. The accused killed him by strangulation. Thereafter, they cut the body into pieces with a sharp cutting weapon and after putting the same in gunny bags, carried them in a van in the night of the following day and left the same at some place. A witness saw those gunny bags and reported the matter to the police. FIR was lodged and case was registered under s. 302/201/341 IPC against unknown miscreants. The prosecution has proved the complete chain of events, including the last seen together theory, the strangulation of the deceased by the accused, and the disposal of the body in gunny bags into a van. The police officer then took the victim to the hospital where he was declared dead. The police officer checked the victim's pockets and found an identity card, which led to the victim's identification. The police officer then lodged a complaint, and an FIR was filed. The investigating officer examined witnesses and recovered weapons, which were sent for forensic analysis. value: The accused, the husband of the deceased, was charged with causing the death of his wife, who died of burn injuries within seven years of their marriage. The prosecution alleged that the deceased was subjected to cruelty and harassment by her in-laws in connection with dowry demands from the initial days of her marriage. It was stated that the in-laws had previously attempted to set her ablaze, but later assured her parents they would not harass her. The deceased was found dead from extensive burn injuries. The trial court convicted the accused under Section 304B IPC and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The High Court, however, converted the conviction to Section 306 IPC and reduced the sentence to five years rigorous imprisonment with a fine of Rs. 1000. The court noted that while there was evidence of cruelty and harassment, there was no specific evidence that the accused demanded dowry, and thus the presumption of dowry death could not be drawn. However, the court found that the accused's actions led to the deceased's suicidal death, and thus the conviction under Section 306 IPC was upheld.

On the day of the incident, the accused's brother informed the victim's brother that the victim had died from an electric shock. The victim's family arrived at the matrimonial home and found her already cremated. The victim's brother lodged an FIR alleging that the accused and his mother had killed the victim for dowry. The trial court acquitted both accused, finding the death accidental. The High Court reversed the acquittal, finding that the victim's death was a dowry death due to the accused's cruelty and harassment, and that the accused failed to rebut the presumption of guilt under the Evidence Act.

value: The accused, a man, was alleged to have engaged in sexual intercourse with the complainant, a woman, on multiple occasions, including on 15.2.2007, under false pretenses of marriage. The complainant initially reported the incident to the police, leading to the registration of a first information report. The accused was arrested and later released on bail. The complainant provided a supplementary statement alleging repeated sexual relations with the accused. The police filed a charge-sheet based on the complainant's statements. However, mobile phone records indicated that the accused was at a different location during the alleged incident, and the complainant was also at a different place. Medical reports did not confirm any physical evidence of sexual assault. The complainant's marital status was later revealed to be married, contradicting her earlier statements. The High Court quashed the criminal proceedings due to lack of credible evidence and the complainant's false allegations.

value: The accused was charged with offences punishable under Sections 302 and 376 of the Indian Penal Code. To prove he was a juvenile at the time of the incident, he submitted a school leaving certificate issued by the Principal of a school. The certificate indicated his date of birth as 10.05.1991. The accused provided testimony from the Head Mistress of the school, who confirmed the authenticity of the certificate. The respondent contested the certificate, leading to an enquiry by the Juvenile Justice Board. The Board sought the opinion of a Medical Board, which opined the accused was approximately 20 years old at the time of the incident. The Sessions Judge set aside the JJ Board's order, directing the case back to the JJ Board for trial. The High Court restored the JJ Board's order, but the Supreme Court overturned the High Court's decision, reinstating the Sessions Judge's order. The Supreme Court concluded that the school leaving certificate was valid and that the accused was a juvenile at the time of the incident, thus the case should be tried by the JJ Board.

value: The accused was alleged to have committed rape on a minor girl. The victim, who was 17 years old at the time of the incident, attempted suicide after the alleged rape and later disclosed the incident to her family and the police. The victim's family reported the case to the police, leading to the registration of an FIR. The victim underwent medical examination, and the medical report indicated that her hymen was intact. The accused was arrested and charged under Section 376 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court convicted the accused and sentenced him to seven years of rigorous imprisonment along with a fine of Rs. 5,000. The High Court upheld the conviction and sentence. The accused appealed, arguing that the delay in lodging the FIR and the medical evidence undermined the prosecution's case. The Supreme Court examined the evidence, including the victim's testimony, the delay in reporting the incident, and the trauma experienced by the victim. The Court found the prosecution's case credible, noting that the delay in reporting the incident and the victim's suicide attempt supported her account of the rape. The Court also emphasized that the amendment to Section 114-A of the Evidence Act supported the prosecution's case, even in the absence of clear medical evidence of rape.

value: The accused, who were involved in a film production, faced a criminal complaint alleging infringement of copyright in the title of a story synopsis. The complainant claimed that the title 'Desi Boys' was used by the accused for their film titled 'Desi Boyz', which was released in 2011. The complainant alleged that the title was the soul of his story and that its use by the accused constituted infringement. The accused argued that the title was not a literary work and therefore not protected by copyright. The case involved a dispute over whether the title of a story could be considered a literary work under copyright law. The accused sought to quash the criminal proceedings, which were dismissed by the trial court. The High Court also dismissed the applications to quash the complaint, stating that the facts would be determined at trial. The Supreme Court ultimately held that no copyright subsisted in the title of the story synopsis and that the criminal complaint was untenable.

value: The Supreme Court applied the principle that suspicion cannot replace proof in criminal cases, and that the prosecution must establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The court emphasized that circumstantial evidence must be conclusive and leave no room for reasonable doubt in favor of the accused.
quote: Suspicion however grave cannot take the place of proof - Prosecution in order to succeed on a criminal charge cannot afford to lodge its case in the realm of 'may be true' but has to essentially elevate it to the grade of 'must be true'. || In a criminal prosecution, the court has a duty to ensure that mere conjectures or suspicion do not take the place of legal proof and in a situation where a reasonable doubt is entertained in the backdrop of the evidence available, to prevent miscarriage of justice, benefit of doubt is to be extended to the accused.

value: The accused, a male, and his co-accused, a female, were charged with the murder of the victim, a male. The victim's body was found hanging from the roof of a shed adjacent to his house. The sole eyewitness, PW1, claimed to have witnessed the incident, which he described as occurring between 1 a.m. and 2 a.m. on the night of 19/20 February 2000. PW1 stated that the accused assaulted the victim from behind, causing him to fall, and then sat on his chest, throttling him while the co-accused covered the victim's mouth. The accused then tied a rope around the victim's neck and suspended his body from the shed. PW1 also alleged an extra-marital relationship between the accused and the co-accused, which was presented as the motive for the murder. The medical evidence indicated that the victim died from asphyxia due to neck constriction, not from hanging. The incident was initially registered as an unnatural death but was later converted into a murder case after six days. The prosecution relied on PW1's testimony, as well as the testimonies of PW5, PW6, and PW8, who learned of the incident from PW1. The trial court convicted the accused under Section 302 IPC, relying on PW1's account and the medical evidence. The High Court affirmed the conviction, accepting the prosecution's claim of motive based on the extra-marital relationship. However, the Supreme Court found PW1's testimony to be unreliable, inconsistent, and improbable, leading to the acquittal of the accused.

value: The accused, a group of sixteen individuals, were alleged to have assaulted and killed the deceased during a dispute over money. The deceased's wife, who was the primary witness, claimed that the accused entered her home, dragged the deceased out, and assaulted him, eventually cutting off his right hand. The deceased's body was found in a field without his hand. The prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence, including witness statements and recovered weapons. However, the witnesses provided inconsistent accounts, and there were no independent witnesses to corroborate the prosecution's case. The medical evidence did not support the claim that the deceased's hand was amputated by the accused. The trial court acquitted the accused due to the lack of conclusive evidence, and the High Court reversed this decision. The Supreme Court reviewed the case and found that the prosecution failed to prove the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt, leading to the restoration of the trial court's acquittal.
quote: For murder of a person – by 16 accused – Trial Court acquitted all the accused – High Court reversed the acquittal order – On appeal, held: Evidence of witnesses were not consistent – There were lot of improvement in the statement of witnesses – There were contradictory statements as regards the number of accused persons involved – All the witnesses were related – Material independent witnesses were not examined – Prosecution failed to prove motive – Panch witnesses as well as medical evidence did not support the prosecution case – Thus, chain of events cannot be said to have been properly brought on record by the prosecution – In view of the shortcomings and discrepancies in the prosecution case, accused persons cannot be said to have formed unlawful assembly with a view to kill the deceased – Guilt of accused not proved beyond reasonable doubt – Acquittal justified.

The prosecution relies on the circumstantial evidence to prove the case. The value of circumstantial evidence rests in its accumulative effect, that is to say, while a single piece of circumstantial evidence may only slightly increase the likelihood that the accused is guilty, several such evidences taken together may carry enough probative force to justify the conviction, if such circumstantial evidence forms an unbroken chain of events resulting in only one hypothesis so canvassed.

value: The case involves an individual who was detained under the National Security Act, 1980. The detention order was initially passed on May 11, 2021, and the individual was detained on May 12, 2021. The order was approved by the State Government on May 13, 2021. The individual submitted a representation against the detention order on May 18, 2021, which was communicated to the State Government and Central Government on May 20, 2021. The Central Government received the representation on June 1, 2021, and the State Government received it on May 24, 2021. The Central Government rejected the representation on June 24, 2021, and the State Government rejected it on July 15, 2021. The individual was not informed of the rejection of the representation until it was communicated to him on June 28, 2021. The Supreme Court held that the delay in considering the representation and the failure to communicate the rejection of the representation violated the individual's constitutional rights under Article 22(5) of the Constitution. The order of detention was therefore invalidated.

value: The accused, who was the husband of the deceased, was alleged to have harassed the deceased due to insufficient dowry. The deceased was admitted to a hospital with severe burns, and a dying declaration was recorded by an Executive Magistrate. The declaration stated that the accused had poured kerosene on her and set her on fire. The deceased's relatives applied for the recording of the statement, and the magistrate recorded it after examining the deceased's fitness. The prosecution relied on the dying declaration and the testimony of the deceased's relatives and a village Sarpanch to establish harassment due to dowry demands. However, the evidence was questioned for its reliability and voluntariness, and the deceased's short temper and the absence of the accused on the day of the incident were noted. The High Court disbelieved the dying declaration in part, and the Supreme Court found that the prosecution failed to prove harassment beyond reasonable doubt.

value: The accused, the wife of the deceased, was charged with abetment of suicide under Section 306 of the IPC. The deceased was found hanging in his home, and the mother of the deceased filed a complaint alleging harassment and abuse by the accused. Colleagues of the deceased also reported incidents of abuse. The accused claimed the deceased had a drinking problem and that the deceased may have committed suicide out of frustration. The police filed a chargesheet against the accused, but the trial court rejected her discharge application. value: The case involves a kidnapping and ransom incident where a minor boy was allegedly kidnapped by a group of individuals. The police received secret information about the incident and registered an FIR based on that information. The grandfather of the kidnapped boy was the first to report the incident to the police, but the police did not investigate thoroughly. The prosecution relied on statements from the kidnapped boy and his father, as well as call detail records, to connect the accused to the crime. However, the investigation revealed inconsistencies in the evidence, including the failure to examine the grandfather as a witness, the lack of convincing evidence linking the accused to the mobile numbers used in the crime, and the improper handling of recovered currency notes. The trial court and High Court convicted the accused, but the Supreme Court found the prosecution's case to be fabricated and the conviction to be unsustainable.

value: The prosecution alleged that on 13.11.2011, at 9:30 p.m., the victim, Narayan Singh, was shot dead at his home in Village Binjana, District Dewas, Madhya Pradesh. The victim's mother, Rachna Bai, testified that she and the victim were sleeping when someone called out the victim's name, prompting him to open the door. A gunshot was heard, and shortly after, a second gunshot struck the victim in the chest, causing him to fall. Rachna Bai saw her daughter-in-law and the victim's son standing on the opposite side of the house and two individuals with their faces covered fleeing the scene on a motorcycle. The prosecution's primary evidence against the appellant was the recovery of a pistol from him and a ballistic report confirming that the bullet recovered from the victim's body was fired from the recovered pistol. There were no eyewitnesses to the crime, and the case against the appellant rested entirely on circumstantial evidence.
